messages.subject: Choosing between spMsPGOcc and sfMsPGOcc
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jeffrey Doser,

I am fitting multi-species occupancy models in spOccupancy with arboreal camera-trap data from the Magdalena Medio region, Colombia. The data are 51 arboreal camera stations (deployed at staggered dates, 83–160 days each) and 4 primate species. Naive occupancy (cameras with detections) is 42/51 for Cebus versicolor, 33/51 for Aotus griseimembra, 15/51 for Alouatta seniculus and 10/51 for Ateles hybridus. I am thinking to use 14-day occasions counted from each camera's own deployment date.
I have two questions:

1) With only N = 4 species, would you recommend spMsPGOcc (one spatial process per species) or sfMsPGOcc with a single factor (q = 1) to account for residual species correlations? I read in Doser et al. (2023) that the factor approach is designed for larger communities, so I am unsure whether it is advisable here. But, in primates in really fragemented areas species correlations can happen.

2) Is there any guidance on how many occurrence covariates are reasonable with 51 sites. I want to include some environmental covariates and some climate covariates. But askingt to IA,it recommends me máximun 4, in particular when one species (Ateles) was detected at only 10 stations.

Thank you very much for your time and for the package.

Best regards,
Karol Aguilar

messages.subject: Re: Choosing between spMsPGOcc and sfMsPGOcc
messages.body_plain:
Hi Karol,

Apologies for the delayed response. Here are some thoughts:

Both the spMsPGOcc and sfMsPGOcc models estimate species-specific effects as random effects. With only four species, you will be estimating random effects with just four levels, which is a challenging estimation task. This can lead often lead to substantial uncertainty in model estimates, and so single-species models may actually be better for your specific scenario. With that said, if you do fit a multi-species model I would recommend using the spatial factor model (sfMsPGOcc) with likely only a single factor.
There is not one size fits all number here, as the ability to estimate covariates also depends on where the detections occur relative to the values of the covariate. Four seems like a reasonable upper bound, but really the best way to test this would be to run some simulations. Regardless of what you choose, I would focus on including covariates that you explicitly hypothesize have some effect on occupancy of the different species, and don't just try to include as many covariates as the data would allow.
Hope that helps,

jeff

messages.body_plain:
Thank you Jeff!

After running a few models though I have found that the same model run multiple times will sometimes converge really well and other times not converge and seems like some chains wander off. For the models where this occurs, the species are quite rare and there aren't many observations or years of data. I believe that specifying initial values may be something that could help with the models converging more consistently. The coefficient that is mixing the slowest is the occurrence intercept, while occurrence covariates have much less trouble, and the detection portion of the model seems to not struggle at all. I find that the highest Rhat and lowest ESS values are for the occurrence variances portion. So I was thinking of starting with only specifying initial values for tau.sq.beta. I have a question though about how the initial values are treated, and specifically in regards to the 'fix' argument. In the documentation I read: "the tag fix can be set to TRUE to fix the starting values across all chains. If fix is not specified (the default), starting values are varied randomly across chains". So if I were to specify inits such as 'tau.sq.beta = c(20, 1, 1, 1, 1)' and have 'fix = FALSE', will this make all the initial values random except for tau.sq.beta? Or will it also randomize the initial values of tau.sq.beta? And if it does, are they fully random from the priors, ignoring the initial values I specify or does it just slightly jitter these values? If it fully randomizes the initial values for everything, is there a way to randomize all except for the ones defined for tau.sq.beta? Additionally, would you expect specifying inits to help convergence vs constraining priors? I was assuming that the inits may be the way to go since the model does converge at least 50% of the time, with the only changes I assume being due to the random initial values since I haven't specified those yet. I appreciate your insight on this, and if I should provide some model summaries or more details for this, I can share those as needed.

Thank you!
Miguel

On Tuesday, October 13, 2026 at 9:25:27 PM UTC-4 jwd...@ncsu.edu wrote:
> Hi Miguel,
>
> Based on what you said, I think a standard (1 | site) random effect is likely suitable for your purposes, although it depends on a variety of factors. WAIC is useful, but its not surprising that you see fairly close WAIC values between these different models given the relatively small sample size in terms of locations for spatial models. If your goal is to solely estimate occupancy at the specific camera trap locations for the different species and you aren't doing prediction at unobserved locations, your estimates between the NNGP model and the (1 | site) model will likely be very similar. So, in practice, while one model might have slightly better WAIC than another, your conclusions would likely be effectively identical, in which case the simpler (1 | site) model would preferred. You should also look at the estimated effective spatial range of the estimated spatial factors. If they all are very small, this indicates there is not much information that can be leveraged across space to improve predictions at unobserved locations, which then minimizes the benefits of the NNGP. If the estimated effective spatial ranges are sufficiently large relative to the distribution of sites in your study area, then that is when the NNGP could prove useful in generating predictions of occupancy probability at new sites. Again, if you're not predicting at new sites, the (1 | site) effect will likely be sufficient. There is not necessarily one right approach, but looking at the predicted occupancy values at the camera locations (which seems like your main objective) and comparing those across models may reveal that the extra complexity provided by the NNGP is not necessary.
>
> Jeff

I think on average, the furthest cameras in my different study locations from each other aren't more than 30km apart. I fit a few different tMsPGOcc and stMsPGOcc models and below are my WAIC values. For the stMsPGOcc, I used n.factors=4, and n.neighbors=5, though not sure how much the models would change by adjusting these parameters.
> >
> > NON-SPATIAL MODELS:
> > tMsPGOcc w/ occu ~ 1 & ar1=F: 11926.4878

> > tMsPGOcc w/ occu ~ (1|year) & ar1=F: 11738.4446
> > tMsPGOcc w/ occu ~ 1 & ar1=TRUE: 11725.4755
> > tMsPGOcc w/ occu ~ (1|site) +  (1|year) & ar1=F: 11603.475
> > tMsPGOcc w/ occu ~ (1|site) & ar1=TRUE: 11594.7365
> > SPATIAL MODELS w/ NNGP=TRUE:
> > stMsPGOcc w/ occu ~ 1  & ar1=F: 11807.2522
> > stMsPGOcc w/ occu ~ 1  & ar1=TRUE: 11804.5163
> > stMsPGOcc w/ occu ~ (1|year) & ar1=F: 11586.645

> > I know that this is just models ran at one of several locations so may not be fully representative of all my data, but my sense is that one unstructured random effect (either site or year) with one structured random effect (ar1 or NNGP) is likely the way to go. These models had 8 years and 13 species. I feel that  "tMsPGOcc w/ occu ~ (1|site) & ar1=TRUE" may be the model I want since I'm not sure how much the NNGP is improving model estimates (the model with the ar1 and NNGP process together seemed to not be the best performing). I know that there are issues with WAIC not being as reliable with hierarchical models with multiple random effect structures so I'm not sure if there is a more preferable method for selecting a model here?
> >
> > I'd be happy to send over any other details that might help with all this as well. I am mainly interested in obtaining the estimated psi values at each camera for the different species, and not really interested in the coefficient responses for this specific work right now. I did run these same models with additional site/year level covariates for the occupancy process and they seemed to lower the WAIC score of each model by 5-10, which has me believe most of the variation is likely not captured by the covariates themselves, and models without covariates could be good for estimating the occupancy values?
> >
> > Thank you!

> > On Wednesday, October 7, 2026 at 5:54:08 AM UTC-4 jwd...@ncsu.edu wrote:
> > > Hi Miguel,
> > >
> > > You should not run models with (1 | site) and NNGP = TRUE, or with (1 | year) and ar1 = TRUE. When you do that, you effectively have two different types of random effects that are trying to explain the same thing (variation across space or variation across time). While in theory they could be estimated given the spatial (NNGP = TRUE) or temporal (ar1 = TRUE) structure, I strongly advise against including multiple forms of site-level effects or multiple forms of temporal random effects in the model at once. In general, using the truly spatial random effects (NNGP = TRUE) to accommodate variation across sites is typically preferred for multiple reasons, particularly if you're doing prediction after fitting the model. Whether using ar1 = TRUE or (1 | year) will largely depend on the size of your data set. With more years, you may see ar1 work better. When you're only working with a handful or so of years, they will likely give very similar results, in which case (1 | year) will likely be favored since it contains one less parameter.
> > >
> > > You are correct that the multi-season multi-species functions do not have k-fold CV functionality built in. The only built-in way in the software to do model comparison for these functions is to use WAIC. However, you can certainly do cross-validation yourself outside of the built-in package infrastructure. This would involve splitting the data set up, running models while holding out part of the data set, predciting at the held out sites, then calculating some comparison metric from the predicted values to compare different model forms.
> > >
> > > Hope that helps,
> > >
> > > Jeff

messages.subject: Model Selection Order and Reporting Covariate Estimates
messages.subject_clean: Model Selection Order and Reporting Covariate Estimates
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jeff,

I am in the process of conducting a stPGOcc() and have a question about the order in which I should be conducting the two sub-models. I have found only a handful of papers that actually explain the order in which they find the top models for their detection and occupancy sub-models. In these examples, they hold a global occupancy model constant to first find the top performing detection model, then hold said detection model constant to find the top performing occupancy sub-model. So the step-wise process would be 1) run all combination detection probability models with global occ model, 2) run all combination occupancy models with top performing detection model from step 1. That makes sense to me, but then in which model do you report your det probability covariate estimates?

For example, if I am looking at the effects of PM2.5 concentration on black bear detection probability, would I report the estimate from the top performing detection sub-model (assuming PM2.5 is in that model) that has the global occ model, or should I instead report estimates from the top performing occupancy sub-model in step 2? I guess my main question is whether the "complete" occupancy model is considered the top model from "step 2." Let me know if I need to clarify anything and thank you for your time!

Best,
Clayton

messages.subject: Re: Unstructured and structured spatiotemporal random effects
messages.subject_clean: Unstructured and structured spatiotemporal random effects
messages.body_plain:
Hi Miguel,

To answer your specific questions about the initial values, if you specify initial values for tau.sq.beta with fix = FALSE, it will use those initial values for tau.sq.beta for the first chain, then it will draw realistic random values from the priors for the additional chains (if you run more than one). There is not a way to randomize all initial values except for tau.sq.beta (or any other parameter).

I would not expect the initial values for tau.sq.beta to really aid in convergence much at all. The fact that the model sometimes converges and sometimes does not converge indicates to me that you have likely overfit the model and are trying to estimate too many parameters given the data set you're working with. So, my recommendation would be to simplify the model until you see more stable convergence.

Jeff

More generally, note that stepwise selection has a fair number of problems so if you haven't already I'd encourage you to read some resources on those limitations prior to interpreting results from the analysis (like this paper <https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1365-2656.2006.01141.x>).

Kind regards,

Jeff

messages.subject: Re: Choosing between spMsPGOcc and sfMsPGOcc
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jeffrey Doser,

Thank you very much for your reply, it was really helpful.

Following your suggestions, I ran a few checks with my data (37 cameras, 4 primate species, 7 occasions per camera):

1. Number of factors. I kept sfMsPGOcc and compared one factor against two. The fit is practically the same (WAIC 715.96 with one factor vs 714.49 with two), the posterior means are very similar, and the same effects are significant in both models. Goodness of fit (Freeman-Tukey Bayesian p-values) is also essentially unchanged.

2. Single-species models. Since you mentioned they could work better with only four species, I also fit one spPGOcc model per species with the same covariates and MCMC settings. All models converged well (Rhat for the occupancy and detection coefficients <= 1.01, ESS > 2,800). The effects have the same signs as in the multi-species model, with somewhat smaller magnitudes, and a few effects that were just significant in the multi-species model become borderline.

3. Covariates. Each occupancy covariate was chosen from an explicit hypothesis (forest cover, canopy height, human footprint, and three climate variables, which I need for the climate projections). I am aware that six is above the four you mentioned as a reasonable upper bound for this sample size, so I interpret the weaker effects with caution. And when I did the simulation for knowing the best models, the six covariates model was the one that best explained data (WAIC)

Given that the conclusions are consistent across all these versions, I will keep the multi-species spatial factor model, with the default priors, as my main analysis and present the other two as robustness checks.

If you think using six covariates is very problematic, just let me know.

Thanks again for your time and for the package.

Best regards,
Karol

On Tuesday, November 10, 2026 at 9:01:15 PM UTC jwd...@ncsu.edu wrote:
> Hi Karol,
>
> Apologies for the delayed response. Here are some thoughts:
>
> Both the spMsPGOcc and sfMsPGOcc models estimate species-specific effects as random effects. With only four species, you will be estimating random effects with just four levels, which is a challenging estimation task. This can lead often lead to substantial uncertainty in model estimates, and so single-species models may actually be better for your specific scenario. With that said, if you do fit a multi-species model I would recommend using the spatial factor model (sfMsPGOcc) with likely only a single factor.
> There is not one size fits all number here, as the ability to estimate covariates also depends on where the detections occur relative to the values of the covariate. Four seems like a reasonable upper bound, but really the best way to test this would be to run some simulations. Regardless of what you choose, I would focus on including covariates that you explicitly hypothesize have some effect on occupancy of the different species, and don't just try to include as many covariates as the data would allow.

messages.subject: Re: Controlling for variable effort in spAbundance - transect.lenghts vs offset
messages.subject_clean: Controlling for variable effort in spAbundance - transect.lenghts vs offset
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jeff,

Thanks for your response! I have a follow up question for you.
You interpreted this correctly - these are point-transects that are surveyed in arid habitats which are not particularly birdy. At the point-level there are relatively few detections of our focal species (lots of 0's), so I want to pool points across transects to get estimates at the transect-level. I see that treating these as "transect" would be inappropriate for estimating a detection function, so I changed transect = "point" and provided an offset vector for the total area of each transect surveyed in each year. For context, these transects are also located in 3 different habitat types (15 transects per habitat; 45 transects total; 20 years of single visit surveys). My abundance formula is ~ Habitat*Year + NDVI + Temp + (1|Transect) and detection is ~ Wind + Temp. My problem is, I've run this global model for several species so far and keep getting a poster predictive check Bayesian p value of 1. I've since added year as a random effect (1|Year), thinking that this would account for some of the temporal fluctuation that the model might not have been catching, but am still getting a p value of 1 for the ppc's. Any thoughts on why this might be?

Thanks!
Taylor

On Wednesday, October 21, 2026 at 3:20:42 PM UTC-4 jwd...@ncsu.edu wrote:
> Hi Taylor,
>
> Thanks for the question, and sorry for the long delay. Here are some thoughts on your design which I think might answer all three questions.
>
> From my understanding, you are working with point count data, where the points counts were distributed along transects, but the distance sampling was done within the individual point count locations. If that is correct, I would suggest modeling the data at the individual point count level such that each row is a point count-year combination. You would then set transect = "point" and offset = the area (in km2) of the point count survey region over which distances were recorded. When doing this, the estimates from mu.samples would be in terms of density (i.e., individuals per km^2), while N.samples would be a per-point/year abundance estimate. See the vignette  <https://doserlab.com/files/spabundance-web/articles/distancesampling>for some more details on the statistical notation for that. If you model at the point-year level, this automatically will account for uneven sampling across years because years in which a given point is not measured simply will not be included in the data set. Also, if you model at the point-level you will want to include a transect-level random effect (i.e., (1 | transect)) and potentially a point count level random effect to account for the repeat measurements of the individual locations over time. If no offset is supplied in this case, then the output will be in terms of number of individuals per point-year. If you did the distance sampling within individual point counts that were clustered together on transects and then tried to model at the transect level, it would be very challenging to define a detection function that made sense. The "transect" term in spAbundance refers to a situation in which distance sampling is conducted by walking along a transect and recording distances to individuals within some band of the transect line. This differs from what I assume your case is, where individual points are where the distance sampling is done and the point locations were sampled to fall along transects.
>
> Hope that helps. Let me know if I interpreted anything about your data set incorrectly.
>
> Jeff
>
> On Tuesday, October 13, 2026 at 3:12:39 PM UTC-4 t...@udel.edu wrote:
> > Hello!
> >
> > I'm using the distance sampling function in spAbundance to get transect-level yearly estimates for a 20 year dataset. I've formatted my data so that every row is a transect-year combination and am including year as a covariate in my models to get at overall trends.
> > The transects in this case consist of points along a line where point counts were conducted, and in some years not all points were visited. I want to account for this variation in effort and have a few questions:
> > 1. If I supply transect.lengths a vector with the length of each transect that was surveyed, will that effectively take care of effort?
> > 2. Am I correct in thinking that if no offset is supplied, the output will be number of individuals per transect? (or in my case transect-year)
> > 3. I would ultimately like the output to be density per square km to be consistent with prior reports - in order to do this would I have to provide a vector of offset values before fitting models (and what would those be in relation to transect lengths?) or alternatively would I manipulate the model output (N.samples?) to calculate density post hoc?
> >
> > Thanks a lot!!
> > Taylor

messages.body_plain:
Hi Taylor,

Thanks for the clarification on the data set, using transect = "point" is the appropriate thing to do in your case.

As far as the high Bayesian p-values go, this could come from a variety of reasons so it's hard to diagnose the cause here. It could come from extra temporal or spatial variation that your abundance model is not accounting for, or it could come from extra variation in detection probability that you're not accounting for. Bayesian p-values can be sensitive to one or a few data points that are predicted very poorly, so it's worth to look into the model fit a bit more. The output object from ppcAbund() consists of the actual posterior predictive check samples that you could explore to see which data points are leading to the poor fit and if there's any patterns among those data points. Because this is count data, you can also calculate fitted values from the model and compare those to the observed values. You can also explore posterior predictive checks grouping by different values (see the group argument), which can help reveal which parts of the data set the model is not fitting well too. I would not recommend fitting a separate model by year and rather would suggest further exploring why the model fit is not ideal by doing what I mentioned in the previous sentences.

If you dig into this a bit and aren't seeing anything obvious then feel free to send me your model off-list and I can take a look.

Jeff
